{{Short description|Mathematical coincidence}}
In [[mathematics]], an '''exceptional isomorphism''', also called an '''accidental isomorphism''', is an [[isomorphism]] between members ''a''<sub>''i''</sub> and ''b''<sub>''j''</sub> of two families, usually infinite, of mathematical objects, which is incidental, in that it is not an instance of a general pattern of such isomorphisms.<ref group="note">Because these series of objects are presented differently, they are not identical objects (do not have identical descriptions), but turn out to describe the same object, hence one refers to this as an isomorphism, not an equality (identity).</ref> These coincidences are at times considered a matter of trivia,{{sfn|ps=|Wilson|2009|loc=[http://www.maths.qmul.ac.uk/~raw/fsgs_files/intro.ps Chapter 1: Introduction]}} but in other respects they can give rise to consequential phenomena, such as [[exceptional object]]s.{{sfn|ps=|Wilson|2009|loc=[http://www.maths.qmul.ac.uk/~raw/fsgs_files/intro.ps Chapter 1: Introduction]}} In the following, coincidences are organized according to the structures where they occur.

== Finite groups ==
The exceptional isomorphisms between the series of [[finite simple group]]s mostly involve [[projective special linear group]]s and [[alternating group]]s, and are:{{sfn|ps=|Wilson|2009|loc=[https://web.archive.org/web/20070824011953/https://www.maths.qmul.ac.uk/~raw/fsgs_files/intro.ps Chapter 1: Introduction]}}
* PSL{{sub|2}}(4) ≅ PSL{{sub|2}}(5) ≅ A{{sub|5}}, the smallest non-abelian simple group (order 60);
* PSL{{sub|2}}(7) ≅ PSL{{sub|3}}(2), the second-smallest non-abelian simple group (order 168) – [[PSL(2,7)]];
* PSL{{sub|2}}(9) ≅ A{{sub|6}};
* PSL{{sub|4}}(2) ≅ A{{sub|8}};
* PSU{{sub|4}}(2) ≅ PSp{{sub|4}}(3), between a [[projective special unitary group]] and a [[projective symplectic group]].

=== Alternating groups and symmetric groups ===
{{see also|The exceptional outer automorphism of S6}}
[[File:Compound of five tetrahedra.png|thumb|The [[compound of five tetrahedra]] expresses the exceptional isomorphism between the chiral icosahedral group and the alternating group on five letters.]]
There are coincidences between symmetric/alternating groups and small [[groups of Lie type]]/[[polyhedral groups]]:{{sfn|ps=|Wilson|2009|loc=Chapter 3}}
* S{{sub|3}} ≅ PSL{{sub|2}}(2) ≅ [[dihedral group of order 6]],
* A{{sub|4}} ≅ PSL{{sub|2}}(3),
* S{{sub|4}} ≅ PGL{{sub|2}}(3) ≅ PSL{{sub|2}}('''Z'''{{hsp}}/{{hsp}}4),
* A{{sub|5}} ≅ PSL{{sub|2}}(4) ≅ PSL{{sub|2}}(5),
* S{{sub|5}} ≅ PΓL{{sub|2}}(4) ≅ PGL{{sub|2}}(5),
* A{{sub|6}} ≅ PSL{{sub|2}}(9) ≅ Sp{{sub|4}}(2)′,
* S{{sub|6}} ≅ Sp{{sub|4}}(2),
* A{{sub|8}} ≅ PSL{{sub|4}}(2) ≅ O{{su|lh=0.9|b=6|p=+}}(2)′,
* S{{sub|8}} ≅ O{{su|lh=0.9|b=6|p=+}}(2).

These can all be explained in a systematic way by using linear algebra (and the action of S{{sub|''n''}} on affine ''n''space) to define the isomorphism going from the right side to the left side. (The above isomorphisms for A{{sub|8}} and S{{sub|8}} are linked via the exceptional isomorphism {{nowrap|SL{{sub|4}}{{hsp}}/{{hsp}}''μ''{{sub|2}} ≅ SO{{sub|6}}}}.)

There are also some coincidences with symmetries of [[regular polyhedra]]: the alternating group A<sub>5</sub> agrees with the chiral [[icosahedral group]] (itself an exceptional object), and the [[covering groups of the alternating and symmetric groups|double cover]] of the alternating group A<sub>5</sub> is the [[binary icosahedral group]].

=== Trivial group ===
The [[trivial group]] arises in numerous ways. The trivial group is often omitted from the beginning of a classical family. For instance:
* C{{sub|1}}, the cyclic group of order 1;
* A{{sub|0}} ≅ A{{sub|1}} ≅ A{{sub|2}}, the alternating group on 0, 1, or 2 letters;
* S{{sub|0}} ≅ S{{sub|1}}, the symmetric group on 0 or 1 letters;
* GL(0, ''K'') ≅ SL(0, ''K'') ≅ PGL(0, ''K'') ≅ PSL(0, ''K''), linear groups of a 0-dimensional vector space;
* SL(1, ''K'') ≅ PGL(1, ''K'') ≅ PSL(1, ''K''), linear groups of a 1-dimensional vector space
* and many others.

== Spheres ==
The spheres ''S''<sup>0</sup>, ''S''<sup>1</sup>, and ''S''<sup>3</sup> admit group structures, which can be described in many ways:
* ''S''{{sup|0}} ≅ Spin(1) ≅ O(1) ≅ ('''Z'''{{hsp}}/{{hsp}}2'''Z'''){{sup|+}} ≅ '''Z'''{{sup|×}}, the last being the group of units of the integers;
* ''S''{{sup|1}} ≅ Spin(2) ≅ SO(2) ≅ U(1) ≅ '''R'''{{hsp}}/{{hsp}}'''Z''' ≅ [[circle group]];
* ''S''{{sup|3}} ≅ Spin(3) ≅ SU(2) ≅ Sp(1) ≅ [[versors|unit quaternions]].

==Classical groups==
{{main|Exceptional isomorphisms of classical groups}}
In addition to Spin(1), Spin(2) and Spin(3) above, there are isomorphisms for higher dimensional [[spin group]]s:
* Spin(4) ≅ Sp(1) × Sp(1) ≅ SU(2) × SU(2)
* Spin(5) ≅ Sp(2)
* Spin(6) ≅ SU(4)

Also, [[Spin(8)]] has an exceptional order 3 [[triality]] automorphism.

In non-Euclidean signature, there are also the isomorphisms
* <math>\mathrm{Spin}^+(1,2) \cong \mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb R)</math>
* <math>\mathrm{Spin}^+(1,3) \cong \mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb C)</math>
* <math>\mathrm{Spin}^+(2,2) \cong \mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb R)\times\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb R)</math>
* <math>\mathrm{Spin}^+(1,4) \cong \mathrm{Sp}(1,1)</math>
* <math>\mathrm{Spin}^+(2,3) \cong \mathrm{Sp}(4,\mathbb R)</math>
* <math>\mathrm{Spin}^+(2,4) \cong \mathrm{SU}(2,2)</math>
* <math>\mathrm{Spin}^+(3,3) \cong \mathrm{SL}(4,\mathbb R)</math>
* <math>\mathrm{Spin}^+(1,5) \cong \mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb H)</math> (i.e., <math>\mathrm{SU}^*(4)</math>)
where <math>\mathrm{Spin}^+</math> refers to the connected component of the identity.

(These group isomorphisms are sometimes presented as central [[isogeny|isogenies]] or isomorphisms of the associated [[Lie algebra]]s instead.)

== Coxeter–Dynkin diagrams ==
{{see also|Klein correspondence}}
There are some exceptional isomorphisms of [[Dynkin diagram#Isomorphisms|Dynkin diagrams]], yielding isomorphisms of the corresponding [[Coxeter group]]s and of polytopes realizing the symmetries, as well as isomorphisms of [[Lie algebra]]s whose root systems are described by the same diagrams.
